title: Why Nvidia Stock Took a Dive Today - The Motley Fool
content: The AI chipmaker sparked renewed fears of circular AI financing. Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) was part of a broad sell-off in the tech sector on Friday, with shares falling as much as 5.3%. As of 2:11 p.m. ET, the stock was still down 5.2%. While the tech downdraft was certainly a contributor, the catalyst that sent the chipmaker lower was the rising cost of artificial intelligence (AI) and the question of who will pay for it all. Reports emerged today that Nvidia may be considering another financing deal with a customer. The company is reportedly in talks to provide billions of dollars in credit guarantees for an Nscale data center that will ultimately be used by Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, which cited "a person familiar with the matter." This marks the latest in a growing string of financing and credit commitments Nvidia has made. For example, reports from earlier this week suggest the company has data center-related commitments and guarantees of $165 billion, according to a report that first appeared in The Information. That's not all. Nvidia also holds more than $63 billion in equity stakes in publicly traded companies, according to a recent regulatory filing. Many of those stakes are in the chipmaker's customers, either directly or indirectly. When you include start-ups, that figure climbs to $99 billion. This has fueled fears among some investors of the repercussions if AI adoption slows or someone builds a better mousetrap than Nvidia's industry-leading graphics processing units (GPUs). If that were to happen, it could be the catalyst that starts the dominoes falling, and the AI trade could all unravel -- or so the popular narrative goes. Yet a look at Nvidia's recent financials should help put those fears to rest. For the company's fiscal 2027 second quarter (ended July 26), the chipmaker generated revenue of $96 billion, up 106% year over year -- and expects that figure to rise to $108 billion when it reports its Q3 results in mid-November. Moreover, Nvidia carries more than $99 billion in cash and marketable securities on its balance sheet, which, in my opinion, provides sufficient liquidity to cover its various financing and credit commitments. We'll have more details when Nvidia releases its next earnings report after the market close on Nov. 17. At less than 26 times earnings, Nvidia stock hasn't been this cheap since 2019. Given its industry-leading position and strong financial position, I'd respectfully suggest that Nvidia stock is a buy. title: Is Nvidia Stock a Trick or Treat? - The Motley Fool
content: It's scary season, but monster growth or a monster correction awaits the market-cap king. With its market-leading $5.2 billion valuation, Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) isn't sneaking up on anybody these days. The poster child of the AI revolution is the largest provider of accelerators and other chips and hardware solutions fueling the AI boom. It has come a long way from its early days, when it largely served gaming enthusiasts. It's playing a bigger game these days, but is the company currently wearing the market-cap crown a trick or a treat as we head into the final two months of this year and beyond? Let's take a closer look at the bad and the good of Nvidia as an investor right now. I'll wrap it up with my own read on where Nvidia stands as a potential portfolio position. There are some compelling knocks on Nvidia despite its stellar growth and compelling forward valuation. I may as well start with the historically cyclical nature of this business. Nvidia has delivered monster growth for years, only to stumble spectacularly. After three consecutive years of delivering 20% to 40% top-line growth, revenue declined 7% in fiscal 2020. I want to cut you off before you blame the COVID-19 crisis. Nvidia's fiscal year ended in January of 2020. The pandemic may have been percolating overseas in the final few weeks of that fiscal year, but the U.S. shutdown didn't take place until mid-March of the 2020 calendar year, a month and a half into Nvidia's fiscal 2021. Nvidia would recover quickly with revenue spurts of 53% and 61% in the two subsequent fiscal years, only to deliver flat top-line growth in fiscal 2023. It's been rolling ever since, but we've seen strong growth come to a grinding halt before. Even strong results sometimes aren't enough. It may surprise you to know that the stock has initially moved lower following four of its last five quarterly reports. Another concern for Nvidia is the sustainability of its recent high-margin results. Nvidia's reported net margin of 64% on a trailing basis can't go much higher. Even its adjusted net margin of 41% is 4 times higher than it was a decade ago. The days of profit growth outpacing revenue gains are possibly numbered. The biggest risk could be the end of the AI revolution itself. It doesn't seem likely right now. AI has changed the way businesses and consumers get stuff done. How can you go back? However, there is the local outcry against data center build-outs. There is also the problematic nature of cyclical financing deals in which Nvidia and others provide clients with the means to bankroll their AI needs. With even the largest tech stars taking hits this earnings season on their soaring capital expenditures, no one would be surprised if things cool down soon. Nvidia stock has delivered generational wealth in recent years. It's an eight-bagger over the last five years, including the slump in fiscal 2023. It also includes this calendar year, in which Nvidia's return roughly matches the market. The stock is slowing at an interesting time. Its business isn't tapping the brakes. If anything, revenue has been accelerating sharply. Nvidia's own guidance models a slowdown for the fiscal third quarter, which it will announce on Nov. 17, but it's hard to scoff at the 89% revenue jump it's projecting for the period. Analysts see a similar leap on the bottom line. The market historically pays a premium for superior growth, but you can buy Nvidia for a mere 13 times next year's Wall Street profit target. Bears will argue that the leading memory stocks that have outgained Nvidia this year are the better value plays. They are trading at mid-single-digit forward earnings multiples, but those are coattail riders with even scarier cyclical volatility. If the market doesn't see value in Nvidia, the cash-rich market-cap king does. Its board of directors recently authorized $150 billion in share repurchases. I'm going with Nvidia as a treat here. The current market sentiment may be gloomy, with shares 15% lower than the all-time high set earlier this month. I'll concede that the lower forward P/E multiples aren't a given. Nvidia has seen its business turn on a dime before. It's juggling a lot right now. I just don't see demand thinning anytime soon. There is also the bullish case to be made that the future may be even better than today's rosy analyst growth projections. The risks of margin contraction are real. Revenue decelerating at this point is a given. Nvidia would be a compelling investment even if its growth were cut in half. It's a treat. Rick Munarriz has positions in Nvidia. title: If AI Spending Slows in 2027, These Semiconductor Stocks Could Hold Up Best - 24/7 Wall St.
content: AI budgets face real pressure heading into 2027, but three chipmakers controlling very different choke points in the supply chain may not feel the pain equally. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) designs the accelerators. Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) supplies the high-bandwidth memory that feeds them. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) makes the leading-edge silicon. 2026's Biggest AI Trends: The Return of CPUs | INTC Stock, AMD Stock, NVDA Stock Year to date, NVIDIA shares are up 16.58%, Micron is up 240.82% and TSMC is up 45.35%. Investors are now asking whether AI budgets can keep growing in 2027. Below, I lay out how each stock could still reach a bold target: $350 for NVIDIA, $1,800 for Micron and $600 for TSMC. The consensus price targets are $328.95 for NVIDIA, $1,561.91 for Micron and $584.39 for TSMC. From current prices, that works out to upside of about 52%, 61% and 33%. Estimates are still going up. Analysts now expect NVIDIA to earn $15.9146 per share in fiscal 2028, up from $12.8148 90 days ago. All three exceeded their most recent EPS estimates. NVIDIA’s $2.22 was its fifth consecutive beat, and Micron’s $33.42 was its eighth. TSMC earned $4.60 per ADR versus $4.46 expected. Beat streaks like these suggest actual results could again come in above forecasts. NVIDIA, at $216.92, trades at about 14x fiscal 2028 estimates. At $350, the multiple would be roughly 22x, in line with the S&P 500’s 21x to 23x. That’s modest for a company expecting revenue growth of approximately 70% next year. At 5x forward earnings, a $1,800 price would put Micron near 10x. TSMC’s 19x forward P/E would rise to about 26x at $600. There are hurdles. TSMC says it is “being prudent in our business planning going into 2027,” and NVIDIA carries $279B in supply commitments. To hit these targets, NVIDIA would need to gain 61%, Micron 85% and TSMC 37%. All three have done far more over five years: NVIDIA returned 773.55%, Micron 1330.97% and TSMC 309.21%. Micron gained 342.12% in the past 12 months alone. At market caps of $5.23 trillion, $1.10 trillion and $2.27 trillion, matching that pace gets harder. Still, these stocks have shown how quickly they get re-rated when earnings beat expectations. If AI spending cools in 2027, I expect TSMC and Micron to hold up best. TSMC has the broadest customer base, and Micron has committed shipments plus tight clean-room supply. NVIDIA has the most upside if demand stays strong, since it trades at a market-level multiple while guiding to approximately 70% growth. All three targets would be harder to reach if the market weakens or hyperscaler spending pauses. title: Why Nvidia shares are down over 4% on Friday? - TradingView
content: Nvidia NVDA shares fell sharply on Friday as a broad selloff in technology stocks intensified concerns over the cost of artificial intelligence infrastructure and the time required for companies to generate returns on their investments. Disappointing results from Amazon and Intel weighed on semiconductor stocks, while fresh reports involving CEO Jensen Huang and regulatory scrutiny of the company's acquisition plans added to the spotlight on the chipmaker. Nvidia was down more than 4.8% trading around $203.40 at the time of writing. The wider market was also under pressure, with the Nasdaq Composite falling nearly 2.5%, while the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average also traded lower. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped around 7% as losses spread across chipmakers. Amazon's third-quarter results added to investor unease over the scale of spending required to build AI infrastructure. The company reported a trailing 12-month free cash flow outflow of $42.4 billion, compared with a positive $14.8 billion in the year-earlier period. It was largely driven by increased investment in property and equipment, primarily for AI. Amazon maintained its capital expenditure outlook of approximately $220 billion for 2026, reinforcing concerns over how quickly its investments will translate into stronger cash generation. Its shares also came under pressure following the results. Intel's weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter guidance further unsettled the chip sector. Although the company beat third-quarter earnings estimates, it forecast revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion for the current quarter, below Wall Street's expectation of around $17 billion. Its adjusted earnings forecast of 25 cents per share also missed the consensus estimate of approximately 43 cents. Intel shares plunged nearly 29%, while AMD dropped around 10%, adding to the pressure on Nvidia and other semiconductor companies. Alphabet's results had already contributed to the technology selloff a day earlier. The Google parent reported third-quarter free cash flow of negative $9.07 billion as capital expenditure on AI infrastructure climbed, while weaker-than-expected advertising revenue added to investor concerns. Report raises questions over Jensen Huang's contact Separately, a New York Times report published Thursday said US intelligence agencies had concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, was allegedly acting as a Chinese intelligence asset and passing commercial information to Beijing. The report said surveillance had revealed that she developed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia rejected suggestions that the interactions were unusual, saying meetings with customers were part of the CEO's job. The company also said regional cloud customers received ordinary business information, not sensitive trade secrets or information relevant to national security. Nvidia is also facing questions from the US Department of Justice over its proposed $12.93 billion acquisition of open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Reuters reported that the department has asked whether the deal could give Nvidia control over an important distribution channel for AI and provide leverage over competitors. The inquiry forms part of a broader examination of Nvidia's acquisitions, investments and sales practices. The DOJ's questions do not establish wrongdoing or mean that legal action will necessarily follow. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Select reference data provided by FactSet. title: Nvidia’s AI Dominance Could Have Further to Run - 24/7 Wall St.
content: NVIDIA just posted another blowout quarter yet the stock sits 11% below its 52-week high, and that gap between fundamentals and price may be exactly the opening bulls have been waiting for. The 24/7 Wall St. price target for NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) is $259.77 over the next 12 months. The stock trades at $216.20, so the target means 20.26% upside. Our model rates the stock a buy with high confidence. Confidence is rated that high because NVIDIA keeps beating estimates and growing faster than the market expects. The recent break in the stock looks like consolidation within an healthy growth story. NVIDIA slipped 0.41% over the past week and 3.94% over the past month. It is up 16.2% year to date. Shares sit about 11% below the 52-week high of $243.37 and 32% above the low of $163.90. Barron’s says mixed big-tech earnings are weighing on the stock. Meanwhile, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is funding its AI buildout, and NVIDIA and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) are reportedly taking a piece of Meta’s new stock offering. The last report tells a stronger story. Fiscal Q2 2027 revenue reached $96.22B, up 105.8% and ahead of the $92.07B consensus. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.22 exceeded the $2.09 estimate. Q3 guidance calls for $108B in revenue. Management expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow approximately 70%, and it calls that a supply-constrained outlook. The chief executive said “The unconstrained number would be a lot higher.” Vera Rubin increases NVIDIA’s revenue opportunity to $40 billion per gigawatt, up from $25 billion for Blackwell. Spending by the top five hyperscalers is expected to approach $1.3 trillion in 2027, and all of that capex has to be powered, cooled and networked by somebody (we rounded up seven suppliers riding that same expansion in a free report on AI infrastructure stocks). Wall Street agrees: 59 analysts rate the stock Buy or Strong Buy, and the consensus target is $328.95. A bull-case estimate puts the stock at $270.57. Gross margins are expected to bottom at 71% to 72% in Q4 as memory costs rise. Supply commitments rose to $279B, and DSO extended to 60 days from 45. Guidance assumes no China data center compute revenue. Some critics also call NVIDIA’s AI lab investments circular financing. Bulls would answer that price increases should raises fiscal 2028 margins back to 72% to 73%, and that most of the inventory build is aimed at the Vera Rubin launch. Even a bear-case estimate of $226.09 sits above today’s price. AMD competes head-on in GPUs, and its Data Center revenue rose 107%. Even so, it trades at a higher multiple than NVIDIA while growing more slowly. Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) is the custom-silicon challenger, with AI revenue up 221%. It trades at a lower multiple, but its revenue base is far smaller. Set against these two, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable. title: Chip Stocks Wipe Out $1 Trillion in Friday Bloodbath: 5 Stocks Alone Account for 60% of the Damage - TradingView
content: Semiconductor stocks lost roughly $1 trillion in market value on Friday, and just five companies did most of the damage. By 11:35 a.m. ET, 23 of the world’s largest chipmakers and equipment suppliers had shed about $1.01 trillion across Wall Street and Asia. Nvidia Corp. NVDA, Intel Corp. INTC, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. AMD, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. TSM and Broadcom Inc. AVGO alone accounted for $610 billion of that, or about 60%. The trigger was Intel. Its shares plunged 28.4% to $65.92 after the chipmaker’s fourth-quarter outlook landed well short of expectations. If the drop holds, it would be the stock’s steepest one-day fall since July 1974. Nvidia led in dollar terms. Its shares fell only 3.6%, yet that move erased about $185 billion, because Nvidia is worth close to $5 trillion. Intel fell nearly eight times as hard in percentage terms. However, it lost less money, about $138 billion. TSMC dropped 5.4%, wiping out roughly $108 billion. Broadcom slid 5.5% and AMD sank 9.7%, and each shed about $90 billion. Elsewhere, SK Hynix Inc. SKHY closed 7.1% lower in Seoul, erasing about $64 billion. Micron Technology Inc. MU, down 5.2%, lost $55 billion. The iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX tumbled 8%, on track for its worst day since early June. The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 7.1%, its second drop of more than 6% in just over a week. Intel’s Data Center and AI division grew revenue 78% to $7.3 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in 15 years. However, shortages of wafers and substrates are capping server shipments, and relief is not expected until the second half of 2027. Meanwhile, the PC business is shrinking. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the roughly $17.1 billion analysts expected. It also warned the slowdown would last through the first half of 2027. The culprit is high memory-chip prices. These are the same prices that lifted SK Hynix, Micron and Sandisk Corp. SNDK this year. Now they are making PCs too expensive to sell in volume. “Intel’s forward outlook proved to be a perfect storm,” Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse said in a note. He called the implied 45% year-over-year collapse in PC units a meaningful surprise. He also cut his price target to $90 from $125 and kept a Neutral rating. Bank of America Securities analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy and cut his price objective to $100 from $145. Arya said strong demand for server processors tied to agentic AI is more than offset by PC and supply headwinds. On Thursday, Alphabet Inc. GOOG suffered its worst day on record. On Friday, Amazon.com Inc. AMZN fell 1.3% after its third-quarter revenue came in slightly below estimates. As a result, investors are again questioning when the hundreds of billions spent on AI infrastructure will pay off. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said on X that AI’s disruption is now visible in tech earnings. He still sees 2027 as the year AI revenue starts to justify the spending. The Nasdaq 100 fell 2.9%, and the S&P 500 lost 1.4%. The 10-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.95%, while the 30-year yield rose 2 basis points to 5.32%. Five stocks generated 60% of Friday’s chip losses. Nvidia's (NVDA) business is booming, but one sector of the market remains a seemingly impenetrable morass for the world's leading chip designer: China. For years, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has struggled to gain a foothold in the world's second-largest economy, due in large part to restrictions imposed by the Department of Commerce, which regulates international chip sales. Seeking inroads, Huang has repeatedly urged the White House to loosen those restrictions, which the administration says are necessary for national security and for the US to remain ahead in the AI race. When Nvidia last reported earnings, forward guidance once again omitted sales projections for China, continually snarled by state politics. The complicated relationship between Nvidia and China was thrust back into public light on Thursday after the New York Times reported new US intelligence efforts. The US intelligence service, the report says, believes a Chinese national named Alice Huang — who has served as a leader of Nvidia chip customer Megaspeed and who maintains a well-documented relationship with Huang himself — has acted as an intelligence asset and passed information to the governing party in Beijing. The reporting raises major questions about potential information leakage from Nvidia to China, not only regarding trade secrets but also about Jensen Huang's increasingly deep ties to the White House as he has lobbied for eased restrictions. At the All-In summit in September, Huang took a call from Trump on stage, putting the US leader on speakerphone as Trump dismissed fears around AI's security implications as a "scam." The race between the US and China to develop and disseminate their own AI technology has, over the past several years, become a paramount concern for the leadership of both governments. While China has matched or even surpassed the US on the development and distribution of "open weight" AI models, which often come at far cheaper costs than "closed weight" alternatives, the US frontier labs such as Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) have retained the lead in developing the most advanced models. Powering those advanced models are chips designed by Nvidia, whose leading semiconductors are often regarded as the gold standard for computing performance. While the chips are hugely popular in the US and other global markets, the Commerce Department has, since 2022, blocked Nvidia from selling successive generations of its chips to Chinese buyers as Washington seeks to maintain its edge over Beijing. Huang won a victory for his company in December 2025 when he secured permission from the Trump administration for Nvidia to export some H200 chips to Chinese buyers, a policy change that came amid a $5 million lobbying push by Nvidia throughout the year. Even chip models such as the H200, which are now several generations behind Nvidia's flagship products, remain competitive for Chinese buyers with options available from companies like Huawei Technologies. Yet H200 sales accounted for less than 1% of Nvidia's $89 billion in data center revenue for the second quarter, Nvidia said. Part of that dearth in sales has also come from Beijing, which recently moved to block Chinese buyers from purchasing Nvidia chips as Xi Jinping's government looks to reduce dependence on US technology, instead turning to homegrown alternatives from the likes of Huawei. Given the "ongoing geopolitical uncertainty," Nvidia CFO Colette Kress told analysts, "there is no China data center compute revenue in our forward outlook." While it's not clear how many H200 chips Nvidia sold to Chinese buyers in the second quarter, those sales fell below the US-approved maximum due to blocks imposed by the Chinese government, the company said. "Under the current rules and geopolitical landscape, we are unable to create and deliver a competitive product for wide distribution in China's data center market with the approval from both the USG and the Chinese government," Nvidia said in its second quarter earnings report. The restrictions haven't stopped Chinese buyers from pursuing workarounds to obtain some of the world's leading chips. Since the US government imposed its sales restrictions on Nvidia, a black-market shadow trade has sprung up in response, according to public reporting and investigations by the Department of Justice. Buyers and sellers throughout Southeast Asian nations not under restrictions import chips under legitimate guises, then switch labels, change packaging, or use other methods to disguise the package's true contents before sending the chips onward into China, reporting and the US government have alleged. Inside China, users on Douyin, the nation's version of TikTok, openly hawk sanctioned chips such as Nvidia's Blackwell B300, priced at millions of US dollars per server, in videos reviewed by Yahoo Finance. Such sales would likely contravene the Commerce Department's restrictions. Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company that employed Alice Huang, has been investigated by US authorities for more than a year due to concerns that the company may be sending Nvidia's most advanced chips to data centers throughout Southeast Asia that serve Chinese companies or directly funneling the physical chips into China through intermediaries, per the New York Times. Nvidia has repeatedly stated that there's no evidence its chips are being smuggled into China, and the company said to the New York Times that if someone close to the company were a "threat to American industry," Nvidia is confident the US government would make the company aware. The company added that while Huang often talks with customers, those conversations never include "information relevant to national security." Even so, for Huang and Nvidia, the headlines come as a reminder of the geopolitical tensions inherent to the AI trade. While it's in Nvidia's interest to serve as wide a customer base as possible, national security concerns in Washington continue to interfere with the company's ability to sell into the world's second-largest economy, where buyers have shown willingness to pay top dollar for its products. Correction: A previous version of this story misstated where Huang took a call from Trump on stage. It was at the All-In Summit. title: Microsoft Just Announced Incredible News for Nvidia Shareholders - The Motley Fool
content: The artificial intelligence (AI) story has been the focus of investors in recent times, but in a different way than in earlier stages of this tech boom. In those initial quarters, investors piled into AI stocks, recognizing the potential of AI to transform businesses and drive earnings growth and share price performance. In many cases, they made the right bet, with hardware and services companies generating explosive growth. Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) has been one of the biggest winners as it dominates the AI chip market. But over the past year, investors have started to worry about the AI story, with the idea that tech giants building out infrastructure may be overspending. This has weighed on the performance of some of these stocks and prompted investors to pay particularly close attention to tech companies' spending plans. Nvidia has continued to report double- and triple-digit growth, but its stock performance hasn't been as eye-popping as in the past. For example, Nvidia stock climbed more than 1,100% over the past three calendar years, but the stock is only up 15% this year. This week, however, Microsoft (MSFT -1.55%) said something that may be seen as quite positive for Nvidia. In fact, the tech powerhouse just announced incredible news for Nvidia shareholders. Let's check it out. We'll start with a quick summary of the Nvidia story so far. As mentioned, Nvidia leads in the AI chip market, selling the fastest graphics processing units (GPUs) around. The GPU fuels key AI tasks, such as training models and inference -- that's the process of actually "thinking" to address a problem. Nvidia entered the market ahead of rivals and has maintained its position through strong customer relationships, its vast ecosystem of products, and constant innovation. All of this has helped power earnings higher, with revenue and profit climbing in the triple digits in the latest quarter. But investors have worried that any potential slowdown in tech spending could significantly hurt Nvidia. After all, data center sales make up 92% of Nvidia's total sales. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,777,360 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Now this brings us to Microsoft, one of Nvidia's biggest customers. You may know this tech company best for its popular software like Word and Excel, but Microsoft is also a massive player in the AI world. Microsoft's cloud business serves a vast array of AI products and services to customers, and the company has been investing heavily in the infrastructure build-out to address growing demand. This week, Microsoft reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings, and as part of the report, it spoke of capital expenditures. Capex has been a major focus for investors, allowing us to monitor the pace of AI growth and better understand levels of demand. Now, here's the good news for Nvidia shareholders. Microsoft said that in the first quarter, about 75% of its capex went toward "short-lived assets," mainly central processing units (CPUs) and GPUs. This suggests significant growth for Nvidia, as a provider of these products. (Central processing units are the main chips found in computers, and Nvidia recently launched its first stand-alone CPU. Prior to this, Nvidia wasn't largely present in the CPU market, but shifted into this area as the CPU emerged as a critical tool powering AI agents.) The news for Nvidia gets even brighter if we look at Microsoft's capex forecasts: The company says that in the second half it expects capex to accelerate, again driven by spending on CPUs and GPUs. Microsoft forecasts $170 billion in capex for the calendar year. And all of this is based on ongoing high demand -- so Microsoft isn't building to serve what might unfold but instead to serve a trend that is already in place. Microsoft, one of Nvidia's main customers, clearly sees high demand for the chip designer's key products and plans to continue spending heavily on them. And that means, even as some market participants worry about the AI spending environment, the actual situation continues to show strength. Nvidia's earnings could continue to roar higher throughout the coming year, and that's fantastic news for shareholders. title: NVDA's Gross Margin Faces Pressure: Can It Offset Rising Memory Costs? - The Globe and Mail
content: NVIDIA Corporation’s NVDA gross margins could face pressure as rising memory costs and supply constraints challenge its ability to maintain strong profitability. However, the company’s pricing power, growing AI demand and shift toward advanced platforms could help offset some of these headwinds. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA reported a non-GAAP gross margin of 75% compared with 72.4% a year earlier and 75% in the previous quarter. Revenues jumped 106% year over year and 18% sequentially to $96.2 billion, while Data Center revenues surged 117% to $89 billion. These figures highlight the company’s strong position in the AI infrastructure market. Still, NVIDIA expects gross margin to decline sequentially to 74% in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, plus or minus 50 basis points. Higher memory prices are a key concern because advanced AI systems require large amounts of high-performance memory. Tight supply could increase component costs and limit production flexibility. NVIDIA has several ways to protect profitability. Its strong relationships with major memory suppliers could help secure supplies, while its advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) and integrated computing systems give it pricing power. The company is also increasing supply and capacity commitments to support future demand. The Vera Rubin platform offers another potential boost. Its improved computing performance and efficiency could help customers justify higher spending on AI infrastructure, supporting NVIDIA’s ability to pass on some cost increases. Overall, NVIDIA’s margins may face near-term pressure, but strong demand and pricing power provide important support. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.AMD and Intel CorporationINTC are expanding their AI businesses, but rising component costs and production challenges could affect their profitability. Advanced Micro Devices reported second-quarter 2026 revenues of $11.54 billion, up 13% quarter over quarter, while its non-GAAP gross margin reached 56.2% compared with 55% in the first quarter. Its Data Center revenues climbed 16% sequentially to $6.7 billion, supported by demand for EPYC processors and Instinct GPUs. However, Advanced Micro Devices’ third-quarter guidance indicates gross margin will remain flat sequentially. title: Can NVIDIA Stock Jump 50%? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. NVIDIA (NVDA) stock trades at 27.0 times earnings. That multiple sits well below the 42.8 average recorded at the end of its last 12 fiscal quarters. Under a Trefis scenario based on NVIDIA’s own figures, the stock would need sales to grow fast enough to offset an even lower multiple in order to jump 50% from its October 28 close of $215.38. So how much could three years of owning the stock make you? Under that scenario, NVIDIA stock would reach about $334.58 a share three years from now, rising 55.3% above today’s price. That return amounts to about 15.8% a year before dividends. The stock’s projected value relies on a simple calculation: revenue times a net margin yields earnings three years out, and those earnings times a P/E determine the price. Here is how NVIDIA stands today against the projections for three years out: All of the gain comes from selling more, though a slightly lower margin and a reduced P/E offset a portion of it. The lower P/E serves as an assumption rather than a finding. Trefis scales today’s P/E to account for the scenario’s slower growth against NVIDIA’s latest 83.4%, keeping the multiple at no less than three quarters of today’s level. Nearly all of NVIDIA’s revenue comes from data centers. Data center sales accounted for $89 billion of the $96 billion total in fiscal Q2 2027, a period that ended in July 2026, management said on the August 26 call. The largest cloud companies bought $49 billion of that amount, and management put the purchases down to sustained strength in Blackwell. Management expects growth to outpace the scenario. The company guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, which sits above the $96.2 billion reported for fiscal Q2 2027. Preliminary expectations for fiscal 2028 point to growth of about 70%, with supply remaining a bottleneck at least through the end of that year. The Trefis scenario projects a slower pace of 30% a year for all three years, because Trefis takes 0.80 times NVIDIA’s latest twelve-month growth and then limits that result to 30%, whereas management’s figure covers a single fiscal year. Management expects its newest data center platform, Vera Rubin, to become the fastest product ramp in NVIDIA’s history. Production shipments began in August 2026 with purchase orders from every major hyperscaler, and management sees Vera Rubin at about 20% of data center revenue in fiscal Q3 2027. Looking at costs, memory prices have risen more than management expected. The company sees gross margin bottoming in fiscal Q4 2027 before NVIDIA’s own price increases take effect. Each row below changes a single assumption while keeping the rest exactly as they appear in the scenario: NVIDIA’s net margin over the latest twelve months is the highest at any of 40 fiscal quarter ends dating back to fiscal Q3 2017. That figure sits well above the company’s average across the 12 quarter ends preceding this latest one. If the other assumptions remain unchanged, revenue growth could slow to 12.2% a year, compared to the 83.4% seen in the twelve months to July 2026, before three years of owning the stock return nothing. The net margin could fall from 63.7% over those twelve months down to 38.6% with the same result. The P/E could drop to 13.0, from 27.0 today, and the gain would also be gone. When the company reports, an event expected in November 2026, NVIDIA’s revenue for fiscal Q3 2027 set against management’s guide is the number to watch. title: Nvidia Shareholders Have a Major Reason to Be Bullish After Jensen Huang's Latest Announcement - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia's evolution into a full-stack AI hardware provider comes with big opportunities. Nvidia's (NVDA -4.22%) GTC Conference in Berlin ran from Oct. 20 through Oct. 22, and CEO Jensen Huang shared some interesting insights into the evolution of the artificial intelligence (AI) market. In addition to expounding on the importance of AI technologies for European countries and companies, Huang detailed the significance of new technologies from his company. Huang's keynote at the GTC event focused heavily on data centers transitioning into "AI factories" -- and he highlighted a new Nvidia product that's set to be central to the transformation. Here's why Nvidia's recent shifts in approach to the AI data center market look like a bullish development for shareholders. Huang used the occasion of GTC to spotlight Nvidia's new comprehensive server racks and their ability to deliver full AI factory performance. The product combines 72 of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) with 256 new custom language processing unit chips. Crucially, the servers aren't just built around its Vera Rubin graphics processing units -- they also include the company's Vera family central processing units (CPUs). Through the integration of the company's CPUs and other hardware, Nvidia sees its monetization of AI compute applications broadening substantially. During the company's recent quarterly call, management said that its sales opportunity per gigawatt of compute has expanded from $18 billion with Hopper to $25 billion with Blackwell to $40 billion with the Vera Rubin family. The big increase in expected sales per gigawatt of compute is being aided substantially by Nvidia's CPU integrations, and the company expects that the increasing importance of AI inference will power new market share gains. While advanced GPUs are the crucial hardware for training advanced AI models, high-performance CPUs can often carry out the inference processes needed to actually run the models in ways that are more efficient in terms of hardware and energy costs. Speaking on the company's new comprehensive server rack product at the company's previous GTC event in March, Huang said, "This is the AI future. This is where AI wants to go. It's designed for inference, this one workload. And this workload is what drives AI factories." Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. At the more recent GTC event in Berlin, Huang said that a 1-gigawatt AI factory would cost operators about $50 billion to set up. Meanwhile, he estimates that such a facility would generate roughly $40 billion in annual revenue, and that delaying bringing the AI factory online by just three months would result in the loss of $10 billion in potential sales. The risk of missing out on tech breakthroughs and revenue has been central to the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure, and it does appear to be a meaningful one. Recent concerns about a valuation bubble in the AI space have created volatility for many stocks in the category, but Huang is highlighting a dynamic that could see players left behind if they don't spend sufficiently on AI compute capabilities. content: Shares of Nvidia Corp (NVDA) slipped 1% on Wednesday  following reports that the U.S. Department of Justice has inquired about how its planned acquisition of Hugging Face could affect competition in artificial intelligence. According to a report from Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, department officials have asked whether the Hugging Face deal would allow Nvidia to control a key distribution point for AI models and tools. The questioning adds to the years-long probe by antitrust regulators on Nvidia’s conduct, which kicked off under former President Joe Biden, the report said. The probe is reportedly continuing with no indication that current President Donald Trump has any involvement. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a relationship with Trump and recently joined the President on his diplomatic trip to China. The DOJ’s recent line of questioning covers the company’s acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether it has pressured customers, sources told Reuters. As part of the probe, the DOJ has reportedly examined Nvidia’s other acquisition deals, including the December 2025 deal to buy SchedMD, sources told Reuters. The department has also scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its licensing deal with chip startup Groq and its acquisition of Run.ai, the report added. Nvidia announced in early September that it had agreed to buy Hugging Face for approximately $12.93 billion. The transaction includes roughly $11.9 billion payable to Hugging Face’s investors and an equity-based retention program of up to about $1 billion for employees who join Nvidia. Hugging Face operates a widely used platform that hosts millions of open-source AI models, datasets, and applications, serving millions of developers and hundreds of thousands of companies. It is often described as a central hub for open AI development. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pledged that the platform will remain open to models, frameworks, clouds, and computing platforms from across the industry, and that Nvidia’s own chips will not be required to use it. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. The central bank held interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4% amid elevated inflation and a strong job market. The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10–2 vote. This move comes as the Fed pivots its attention to inflation amid energy price fluctuations from the conflict in Iran, while the job market remains resilient. “Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed statement said. “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. Under Warsh’s revamped framework, the FOMC will issue rate decisions at seven of its eight scheduled sessions in 2027, reserving one meeting exclusively for broad monetary policy strategy without issuing a formal rate statement. By 2028, the central bank plans to reduce its rate-setting votes to six per year, leaving two gatherings devoted entirely to strategic evaluations. Much of this volatility isn't Nvidia's fault. Rather, it's the result of an investor rotation away from artificial intelligence (AI)-related tech giants and toward more defensive offerings. That's dirt cheap, by most historical measures, and suggests the market thinks that some sort of significant slowing may be on the horizon. Especially if Nvidia can continue to grow its overall market share in the world of semiconductors simply by producing the fastest and best next-generation semiconductors. Still, I'd also suggest that spending overhangs from some of Nvidia's key clientele could see them start to pull back on spending. That's what the data suggests, and if that does happen, many of the same scenarios we saw play out a little less than 30 years ago during the dot-com era could be at play once again. We'll have to wait and see. But I think a price target closer to the Street-low of $180 per share is much more likely than the Street-high target of $515 for NVDA stock. content: AI tailwinds continue to propel the world's leading data center chipmaker, but can the stock keep climbing? With a market cap of about $5.3 trillion, Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) is the largest company in the world -- and it's easy to see how it reached that size. The tech giant's advanced processors are the dominant compute hardware in the data centers that underpin the entire generative artificial intelligence (AI) industry, and as soaring demand for its chips continues to outstrip supply, it enjoys booming sales at sky-high margins. That said, all investors know that past performance doesn't guarantee future results. And the larger a company becomes, the harder it is for additional growth to move the needle on its finances. So what might this leading tech stock be worth by the end of 2027? It's been roughly four years since OpenAI's ChatGPT introduced the world to the power of generative AI, and the revolution that it triggered shows no signs of slowing down. According to analysts at Goldman Sachs, tech companies' AI-related capital expenditures will total more than $1 trillion in 2026. And much of that spending will go toward graphics processing units (GPUs) and other data center compute hardware created by companies like Nvidia. The supply of advanced semiconductor equipment remains tight relative to demand, and Nvidia's GPUs remain the most popular data center AI accelerators, a situation that allows it to charge high prices. These persistent tailwinds were reflected in the company's second-quarter earnings. Revenue jumped 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, driven mostly by strength in the company's data center segment, which grew 117%. This business involves designing and selling advanced AI infrastructure. And management plans to keep the momentum going with new releases, such as its Vera Rubin platform, which is designed specifically to handle agentic AI workloads. Nvidia's bottom line is also looking good; the company's net income jumped 32% year over year to $59.7 billion in the period. On the surface, Nvidia looks like the perfect stock to own. But investors should be aware that it faces some big challenges. Perhaps the biggest is its lack of diversification. In the past, Nvidia boasted a broader business model as it sold GPUs for consumer video games, machine learning, cryptocurrency mining, virtual reality devices, and data centers, among other uses. However, the mix of end-uses has condensed dramatically: Data centers now account for over 90% of its revenue. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. This situation leaves Nvidia exceptionally exposed to a potential downturn in the AI market. And even the bulls should be willing to accept that the current levels of data center spending probably won't last forever. A recent paper by Columbia University finance professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh (first presented at the nonpartisan Brookings Institution) concludes that U.S. businesses and consumers will eventually have to spend the equivalent of 9% of the country's GDP on AI-related services to justify the current levels of capital investment going toward the technology. That's as much as we spend on food, and far more than we spend on essentials like energy and construction. While large language models (LLMs) are useful, they are notoriously difficult to monetize due to their huge energy consumption and the intense level of competition in the space, especially from lower-cost Chinese alternatives. In fact, industry leader Anthropic reported an eye-popping net loss of $80 billion in the first half of 2026. If the consumer-facing side of the AI market struggles to turn a profit, that could eventually lead to a smaller market for hardware providers like Nvidia. Trading today at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 23.5, Nvidia stock is still relatively cheap relative to its growth potential. And investors who believe the AI boom will maintain its momentum can comfortably expect the stock to offer additional multibagger returns from here. That said, this represents the best-case scenario. And there are several reasons to be less optimistic. The AI industry shows many of the signs that it's in an unsustainable bubble. And Nvidia's business model isn't diversified enough to be cushioned against the painful impact of a spending slowdown. With these risks in mind, it looks more likely to me that when we get to the end of 2027, Nvidia shares will be trading close to flat compared to their price today. Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) fortunes have been lifted remarkably by the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Over the past three years, during a period when data center spending among hyperscalers really kicked into high gear, the company's shares have rocketed 410% higher (as of Oct. 23). Since it produces the most advanced and most popular graphics processing units for AI data centers, it has benefited like no other business has. This AI stock is trading at around $211 right now. If you buy $10,000 worth of Nvidia shares today, I predict that it will grow remarkably by 2029 -- if the AI spending boom holds up. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The consensus estimate of the sell-side analyst community is that Nvidia's earnings per share will increase at a compound annual rate of 65% from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2029. This doesn't look like a stretch. Between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, that profitability metric climbed at a yearly clip of 204%. That was certainly the most powerful tailwind driving the stock higher. If Wall Street's forecast proves correct, then Nvidia's share price should mimic this bottom-line gain. That would turn a $10,000 investment in the chipmaker made today into a position worth $45,000 in three years. A 350% return in 36 months is impossible to complain about. This premise assumes that the company's valuation multiple doesn't change. Nvidia stock currently trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 26.7. This bull case is definitely within the realm of possibility. Indeed, while it may sound hard to believe, if the stock does rise at 65% annually between now and late 2029, it would result in a slightly lower rate of return than the business posted over the prior three years. However, for that to occur, Nvidia will need the AI industry's momentum to continue. It all comes down to AI-related spending. While Nvidia can still prosper even if it slows down slightly, it can't decelerate too much. According to a forecast from investment firm Vanguard (itself a giant with $13 trillion in assets under management), the five big hyperscalers, which represent a significant customer cohort for Nvidia, will spend more than $1 trillion on AI capex each year from 2027 through 2030. The bear case also shouldn't be ignored, though. The amount of capital flowing through the AI industry, coupled with the speed of model development, is unprecedented. While AI looks like it could be a revolutionary technology, no one has a clue how its adoption will play out, or to what degree those investments will pay off. These innovative capabilities don't mean that the infrastructure providers -- or the hardware giants that support them -- will continue to be winners. If at some point in the coming years, AI infrastructure spending slows down dramatically faster than the market currently expects, Nvidia could be in trouble. Under that scenario, demand for its GPUs would fall, taking the wind out of its jaw-dropping revenues and profits. This could happen because of softening end-user demand for AI models. There could also be cracks forming in the complex web of financing between the key players in the space. Additionally, emerging competitive threats to Nvidia's dominant position in the AI accelerator market coming from peers are something investors need to keep tabs on. The chips being developed by both its longtime peers and some of its largest hyperscaler customers could materially eat away at Nvidia's share of the data center chip market. Under that downbeat scenario, it's possible that its EPS will only grow 15% or 20% per year. And the earnings multiple the stock trades at could contract as growth investors head for the exits. If negative sentiment hits Nvidia, it will surely spread through the market and impact other AI stocks. Because of how concentrated the value of the stock market is right now in companies connected to the AI trend, such a retreat could crush equities broadly. And that would resemble a bubble bursting. Given how much momentum the AI ecosystem seems to have, investors may struggle to envision the bear case becoming a reality. Pay close attention to hyperscalers' capital expenditures. Revenue trends at AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI are also worth watching. Weakness there might indicate that things are cooling down. Between the bear and bull cases, I still lean toward the former. However, I accept that uncertainty is extremely high.
